question: What is the form and root of damāʾ?

positions.position: The singular of «الدماء» is «دم»; no noun has only two letters without an omitted letter, here a yāʾ retained in poetic usage.
positions.reasons: NAHHAS (author): The singular of «الدماء» is «دم»; no noun has only two letters without an omitted letter, here a yāʾ retained in poetic usage.

positions.position: The singular dam has a deleted final letter, said to be ya; its original form appears in the poetic dual al-damiyan, showing that the noun was not originally only two letters.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL (author): The singular dam has a deleted final letter, said to be ya; its original form appears in the poetic dual al-damiyan, showing that the noun was not originally only two letters.

positions.position: Damāʾ is the plural of dam; its omitted final weak radical may be yāʾ or wāw, as shown by damiyān and damwān.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): Damāʾ is the plural of dam; its omitted final weak radical may be yāʾ or wāw, as shown by damiyān and damwān.

positions.position: The language also attests shortening and consonant doubling for dam, while grammarians differ over the deleted radical's original vowel pattern.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): The language also attests shortening and consonant doubling for dam, while grammarians differ over the deleted radical's original vowel pattern.

positions.position: دماء is the plural of دم; a declinable noun cannot consist of two letters, so the third radical, its final letter, is omitted.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (author): دماء is the plural of دم; a declinable noun cannot consist of two letters, so the third radical, its final letter, is omitted.

positions.position: The deleted radical may disappear and دم be used as shortened دما, as in the cited poem.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (author): The deleted radical may disappear and دم be used as shortened دما, as in the cited poem.

question: Why single out bloodshed and repeat “therein”?

positions.position: They explain corruption as sins and bloodshed as spilling blood without right.
positions.reasons: THALABI (author): They explain corruption as sins and bloodshed as spilling blood without right.

positions.position: Because yufsid is affirmative and does not imply every kind of corruption, the angels name bloodshed as the gravest form, which destroys God's created bodies.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): Because yufsid is affirmative and does not imply every kind of corruption, the angels name bloodshed as the gravest form, which destroys God's created bodies.

positions.position: Repeating fīhā after corruption highlights the reversal of a place of worship into one of wrongdoing; the parallel is 2:11, while omission after bloodshed avoids three repetitions.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): Repeating fīhā after corruption highlights the reversal of a place of worship into one of wrongdoing; the parallel is 2:11, while omission after bloodshed avoids three repetitions.

positions.position: Repeating the locative phrase emphasizes how implausible the angels find the prospect of corruption on earth.
positions.reasons: BURSEVI (author): Repeating the locative phrase emphasizes how implausible the angels find the prospect of corruption on earth.

positions.position: The angels mean unjustly spilling blood, and the wording names bloodshed because it is the ugliest kind of killing.
positions.reasons: BURSEVI (author): The angels mean unjustly spilling blood, and the wording names bloodshed because it is the ugliest kind of killing.

question: How does “while we” attach syntactically?

positions.position: The wāw is circumstantial: ‘Would You appoint one while we are more deserving of favor?’
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF-FULL (author): The wāw is circumstantial: ‘Would You appoint one while we are more deserving of favor?’

positions.position: This circumstantial clause explains the question as a friend asking why a trusted stranger is favored: why appoint sinners when we are sinless and more entitled? Its purpose is to ask what favors humans, not to
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI-FULL (author): This circumstantial clause explains the question as a friend asking why a trusted stranger is favored: why appoint sinners when we are sinless and more entitled? Its purpose is to ask what favors humans, not to boast.

positions.position: The waw in ونحن is circumstantial, and بحمدك is also circumstantial: the angels glorify while praising God.
positions.reasons: NASAFI-FULL (author): The waw in ونحن is circumstantial, and بحمدك is also circumstantial: the angels glorify while praising God.

positions.position: The circumstantial clause wa-naḥnu nusabbiḥu has several reported senses: divine transcendence (Qatāda), remembrance aloud (al-Mufaḍḍal), humility (Ibn al-Anbārī), or prayer (Ibn Masʿūd and Ibn ʿAbbās).
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): The circumstantial clause wa-naḥnu nusabbiḥu has several reported senses: divine transcendence (Qatāda), remembrance aloud (al-Mufaḍḍal), humility (Ibn al-Anbārī), or prayer (Ibn Masʿūd and Ibn ʿAbbās).

positions.position: نقدس coordinates with نسبح and is a predicate of نحن; its omitted object is ourselves and our actions.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (author): نقدس coordinates with نسبح and is a predicate of نحن; its omitted object is ourselves and our actions.

positions.position: The wāw is circumstantial; ونحن نسبح is a nominal clause in the accusative as a circumstantial clause.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (author): The wāw is circumstantial; ونحن نسبح is a nominal clause in the accusative as a circumstantial clause.

positions.position: Ibn ʿAṭiyya accepts placing ونحن نسبح inside an implied question: وأنحن نسبح أم نتغير.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (ابن عطية): Ibn ʿAṭiyya accepts placing ونحن نسبح inside an implied question: وأنحن نسبح أم نتغير.

positions.position: The third category is wāw of circumstance, which enters a nominal clause, as in the angels' “while we glorify You.”
positions.reasons: ITQAN (author): The third category is wāw of circumstance, which enters a nominal clause, as in the angels' “while we glorify You.”

positions.position: It is not established that a nominal clause used as an emphatic circumstantial clause must omit its pronoun and conjunction; al-Alusi cites Sharh al-Tashil.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): It is not established that a nominal clause used as an emphatic circumstantial clause must omit its pronoun and conjunction; al-Alusi cites Sharh al-Tashil.

question: What do the angels imply by contrasting their worship?

positions.position: Abū ʿAlī says they asked to be placed on earth because it would benefit them.
positions.reasons: JISHUMI (أبو علي): Abū ʿAlī says they asked to be placed on earth because it would benefit them.

positions.position: They may ask for earth, or part of it, for themselves if beneficial; God chose heaven for angels and earth for people, for their religious good.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): They may ask for earth, or part of it, for themselves if beneficial; God chose heaven for angels and earth for people, for their religious good.

positions.position: The wāw in ‘and we glorify’ is circumstantial, like saying, ‘Would you favor someone while I am more deserving of favor?’
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The wāw in ‘and we glorify’ is circumstantial, like saying, ‘Would you favor someone while I am more deserving of favor?’

positions.position: The angels’ question expresses their claim to greater entitlement to the caliphate and asks why humans were preferred despite their expected corruption.
positions.reasons: BURSEVI (author): The angels’ question expresses their claim to greater entitlement to the caliphate and asks why humans were preferred despite their expected corruption.

positions.position: The angels offer themselves as God's successors, or ask Him to appoint them, questioning the benefit of an earthly successor.
positions.reasons: TABATABAI (author): The angels offer themselves as God's successors, or ask Him to appoint them, questioning the benefit of an earthly successor.

positions.position: Angels inhabit heaven, Adam and descendants earth, including worshippers.
positions.reasons: MUQATIL (author): Angels inhabit heaven, Adam and descendants earth, including worshippers.

positions.position: Angels remember God, pray and magnify His command; compare thunder in 13:13.
positions.reasons: MUQATIL (author): Angels remember God, pray and magnify His command; compare thunder in 13:13.

positions.position: On the prayer interpretation, the angels pray and recite the Opening of the Book in their prayer.
positions.reasons: THALABI (author): On the prayer interpretation, the angels pray and recite the Opening of the Book in their prayer.

positions.position: Without God’s grace through guidance and kindness, the angels could not worship Him.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF-FULL (author): Without God’s grace through guidance and kindness, the angels could not worship Him.

positions.position: The angels' praise is compared with the wording about angels praising their Lord in 42:5.
positions.reasons: TABRISI (author): The angels' praise is compared with the wording about angels praising their Lord in 42:5.

positions.position: Despite abundant worship and never slipping, angels remain fearful and apprehensive of God.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Despite abundant worship and never slipping, angels remain fearful and apprehensive of God.

positions.position: They explain the angels’ words as saying that they pray to God.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR-FULL (السدي عن ابن عباس وابن مسعود وغيرهما من الصحابة): They explain the angels’ words as saying that they pray to God.

positions.position: Alternatively, the angels mean “Glory be to God and praise be to Him.”
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (قيل): Alternatively, the angels mean “Glory be to God and praise be to Him.”

question: What does the angels' tasbīḥ mean?

positions.position: Tasbīḥ is glorification and exaltation
positions.reasons: ABDURRAZZAQ (author): Qatada glosses tasbih as glorification. TAB-FULL (بعض أهل العربية): Some Arab grammarians say the question was not a protest against God but a request to learn; the angels mentioned their own glorification because they disliked disobedience after the jinn had disobeyed. TAB-FULL (قتادة): Qatada takes tasbih here in its familiar, literal sense of glorification. TAB-FULL (أبو ذر): Abu Dharr reports that when asked which words God loves most, the Prophet named the words God chose for the angels: repeated glorification of the Lord with praise. TAB-FULL (author): Al-Tabari explains that the angels wondered at a creation that would sin and implied that they themselves glorified, prayed to, and obeyed God. SULAMI (الواسطي): Whoever says “I” contests divine power; the angels' boastful claim to glorify God also objected to lordship, despite being a setting for divine instruction. MAWARDI-FULL (المفضل): Al-Mufaḍḍal takes it as the familiar act of tasbīḥ, citing Jarīr’s verse about pilgrims glorifying God. MAWARDI-FULL (author): Though others may be described as pure, tasbīḥ is a religious term for the highest degree of exaltation, due only to God. MAWARDI-FULL (مجاهد): Mujāhid understands it as glorifying God. QUSHAYRI (author): God drew out the angels’ concealed self-admiration in their worship, making them disclose their hidden thoughts by citing their glorification. QUSHAYRI (author): Angelic glorification has no significance without God’s favor, and human sins cause no harm when met by His pardon. QUSHAYRI (author): The angels’ glorification displays their deeds and merit, while forgiveness of human sins displays the Creator’s generosity and mercy. QUSHAYRI (author): God needs no worship; their glorification establishes their own praise, while His forgiveness establishes the Creator’s praise. QUSHAYRI (author): God knows humans’ humbled, broken hearts despite their bad deeds, whereas angels’ hearts become proud when they display glorification. WAHIDI-BASIT (author): Another explanation is that the angels wondered whether the successor would be from the jinn, whose predecessors corrupted the earth, or from the angels, who glorify God; God did not reveal that Adam’s descendants would include both obedient and disobedient people. WAHIDI-BASIT (author): The word's root means distancing; anyone praising God and distancing Him from evil has glorified and purified Him. WAHIDI-BASIT (بعض أهل المعاني): Some linguists explain tasbih with praise as speaking God's praise: praise and gratitude themselves honor Him and acknowledge His worthiness to be purified and exalted. JISHUMI (author): Another account says glorification benefits the angels, while their ability to perform it comes from God’s enabling. JISHUMI (author): One rejects that they asked to replace people because this implies a divine will without evidence; another rearranges the phrase to mean they glorify by God’s guidance and then praise Him. JISHUMI (قتادة): Qatāda interprets the angels’ tasbīḥ as the familiar act of glorification. IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): Glorifying God with praise means declaring Him free of what is unfitting to His essence and attributes. IBNATIYYA-FULL (بعض المتأولين): Some read “while we glorify You” as a question about whether angels should continue in that state or change from it; Ibn Atiyya says this suits a strictly interrogative reading. IBNATIYYA-FULL (قوم): Some understand the angels to mean that if God had appointed them to succession on earth, they would glorify Him; this suits the astonishment reading. TABRISI (مجاهد): Mujahid says praising God is tasbih because praise exalts Him and recognizes He deserves glorification. RAZI-FULL (author): Angels are honored, do not disdain worship, and glorify God day and night without tiring. RAZI-FULL (علي): Ali describes angels in varied worship postures, glorifying tirelessly without sleep, lapse, bodily fatigue, or forgetfulness. RAZI-FULL (المخالف): An opponent says the angels' self-praise and claim of exclusive glorification resemble conceit and backbiting. RAZI-FULL (author): Uninterrupted glorification day and night is incompatible with committing sin. RAZI-FULL (author): One explanation is that glorifying God with praise recognizes that his praise and majesty make him deserving of glorification. RAZI-FULL (author): A second explanation is that people can glorify God only through his enabling grace, as David’s example illustrates. RAZI-FULL (author): Their self-praise may itself amount to glorifying themselves; later humans will instead humble themselves by confessing wrong and asking mercy. RAZI-FULL (المعتزلة): The Muʿtazilites argue that the angels attribute their glorification and purification to themselves; if God did those deeds, there would be no merit in them over bloodshed. QURTUBI-FULL (المفضل): Al-Mufaddal says the angels' tasbih is raising the voice in remembrance, supported by Jarir's line about pilgrims glorifying and proclaiming God's greatness. BAYDAWI-FULL (author): We purify our souls from sins for Your sake; the angels set glorification against the corruption (understood by some as idolatry) and purification against the grave vice of bloodshed. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): Another proposed complement contrasts the question with the angels' state: will You change us, though we glorify You? ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): In bi-ḥamdika, the bāʾ can mark accompaniment: the angels glorify while joined by praise, a circumstantial phrase within another circumstantial phrase. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (صفي الدين أبو عبد الله الحسين ابن الوزير أبي الحسن علي بن أبي المنصور الخزرجي): The author of Fakk al-Azrar assigns the apparent objection to Iblis and the glorification and obedience to the angels, who had first spoken in a collective answer. DURR-FULL (أبو صالح): Abu Salih glosses the angels' words as magnifying and glorifying God. ALUSI-FULL (أهل الله): Their cosmology next describes absolute darkness receiving light, the Throne appearing with the Merciful's manifest Name, and surrounding angels whose sole occupation is glorification. ALUSI-FULL (author): The first group are the exalted and proximate angels, constantly glorifying God without fatigue. ALUSI-FULL (صفي الدين الخزرجي): Al-Khazraji says the speakers differ: Iblis, included among the angels, voiced the objection, while the other angels voiced glorification after his refusal separated him from them; al-Alusi calls this an interpretive gloss, not tafsir. ALUSI-FULL (author): Putting the subject before the verbal predicate conveys restriction: the angels, in contrast to the proposed vicegerent, glorify God. ALUSI-FULL (author): If “Your praise” is construed as an objective genitive, the angels mean that they praise God because He enabled them to glorify Him. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR (author): Another class surrounds the Throne and glorifies God. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): He rejects reading the angels’ glorification as a question with an omitted interrogative and an omitted alternative, since the syntax gives no evidence for either deletion.

positions.position: Tasbīḥ denotes prayer
positions.reasons: AKHFASH (author): Remembrance and prayer can be tasbih; glorification is accompanied by praise, with 40:7 and 110:3. TAB-FULL (author): In Arab usage, remembrance and prayer can be called tasbih; the report also records the angels’ repeated phrase of glorification with praise. TAB-FULL (author): Al-Tabari reconciles prayer and glorification with purification: prayer magnifies God and cleanses him of the false attributions made by disbelievers. ZAJJAJ (author): Any act intended for God may be called tasbīḥ; completing prayer is one Arabic use of tasbīḥ. THALABI (الحسن): Al-Hasan says the angels utter “Glory and praise belong to God”; this is the creatures’ prayer and glorification, through which they receive provision. THALABI (author): Another interpretation takes tasbih as prayer commanded by God; prayer is called subha. MAWARDI-FULL (ابن عباس وابن مسعود): Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Masʿūd interpret the angels’ tasbīḥ as prayer. WAHIDI-BASIT (author): Tasbih means declaring God free of every evil, and it can also mean prayer; to glorify God is to pray to Him. JISHUMI (ابن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbās interprets the angels’ tasbīḥ as prayer. BAGHAWI-FULL (قيل): Another explanation is that the angels mean they pray in accordance with God's command; Ibn Abbas says tasbih throughout the Quran means prayer. IBNATIYYA-FULL (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas and Ibn Masud say the angels’ glorification is their prayer to God. RAZI-FULL (ابن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Masʿud interpret ‘we glorify’ as ‘we pray,’ taking tasbih to mean prayer. QURTUBI-FULL (ابن مسعود): Ibn Masʿud and Ibn ʿAbbas interpret the angels' tasbih as prayer, citing the description of Jonah as one of the tasbih-makers in 37:143. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): Tasbīḥ is speech, or speech with action, that magnifies and declares God free of deficiency; hence remembrance and prayer can be called tasbīḥ.

positions.position: Tasbīḥ declares God free of imperfection
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (author): Al-Tabari glosses tasbih with praise as magnifying God through praise and gratitude; he also defines its root sense as declaring God free of attributes unworthy of him. ZAJJAJ (author): To glorify God with praise means to declare Him free of evil. ZAJJAJ (سيبويه وغيره من النحويين): Sībawayh and other grammarians gloss subḥān Allāh as declaring God free of evil and exalting Him above it. MAWARDI-FULL (author): Tasbīḥ is declaring God free of evil in a mode of exaltation; al-Aʿshā’s line uses subḥān as disavowal. WAHIDI-BASIT (الأزهري): Al-Azhari says exegetes and linguists agree that tasbih means declaring God transcendent and free of evil. RAZI-FULL (أهل التذكير): Ahl al-tadhkir say tasbih in the Qur’an can mean transcendence: God has no peer, administers the heavens and worlds, is above wrong descriptions, self-sufficient and sovereign, all-knowing, and without consort or child. QURTUBI-FULL (author): The angels' tasbih means declaring God exalted above what does not suit His attributes; in Arabic it is magnifying Him by declaring Him free of evil, as al-Aʿsha's line uses subhan for disavowal. SAMIN-DURR (author): تسبيح means declaring transcendence and disavowal; its root سبْح denotes distance, as in swimming. SAMIN-DURR (author): سبحان الله declares God transcendent and free of what does not befit Him; the poem uses سبحان من علقمة for تنزيها.

positions.position: Al-Tabari says tasbih fundamentally declares God free of attributes that do not belong to him; al-Asha’s verse means, reproachfully, ‘Glory be to God against alqama’s boasting.’
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (author): Al-Tabari says tasbih fundamentally declares God free of attributes that do not belong to him; al-Asha’s verse means, reproachfully, ‘Glory be to God against alqama’s boasting.’

positions.position: Al-Aʿshā’s line uses the word سبحان to mean disavowal of ʿAlqama and his boasting.
positions.reasons: ZAJJAJ (author): Al-Aʿshā’s line uses the word سبحان to mean disavowal of ʿAlqama and his boasting.

positions.position: Al-Hasan explains the angels' phrase as saying, Subhan Allah wa bihamdihi.
positions.reasons: WAHIDI-BASIT (الحسن): Al-Hasan explains the angels' phrase as saying, Subhan Allah wa bihamdihi.

positions.position: Subhan Allah means God's freedom from evil and became an exclamation of wonder; al-A'sha's verse uses it to express astonishment.
positions.reasons: WAHIDI-BASIT (author): Subhan Allah means God's freedom from evil and became an exclamation of wonder; al-A'sha's verse uses it to express astonishment.

positions.position: Tasbīḥ and taqdīs mean declaring God far removed from evil; their roots also convey going far away.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF-FULL (author): Tasbīḥ and taqdīs mean declaring God far removed from evil; their roots also convey going far away.

positions.position: Qatada takes tasbih in its ordinary linguistic sense: saying “subhan Allah.”
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL (قتادة): Qatada takes tasbih in its ordinary linguistic sense: saying “subhan Allah.”

positions.position: Muqātil interprets their tasbīḥ as saying ‘subḥāna Allāh.’
positions.reasons: IBNJAWZI-ZAD (مقتادة): Muqātil interprets their tasbīḥ as saying ‘subḥāna Allāh.’

positions.position: Al-Rāzī says the preposition bi in the angels' tasbīḥ requires grammatical analysis to determine what it attaches to.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Al-Rāzī says the preposition bi in the angels' tasbīḥ requires grammatical analysis to determine what it attaches to.

positions.position: God needs no creatures’ tasbih;
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): God needs no creatures’ tasbih; because nonliving things do not need its reward, God gives their reward to the human who serves him, showing that the whole world can be put at the servant’s service.

positions.position: They urge tasbih for divine favor and relief, including seeking God’s pleasure and praising him morning and evening.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (أهل التذكير): They urge tasbih for divine favor and relief, including seeking God’s pleasure and praising him morning and evening.

positions.position: Tasbih and taqdis mean distancing God from what is evil or unfitting.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Tasbih and taqdis mean distancing God from what is evil or unfitting.

positions.position: Distance from evil is tasbih; distance from good is a curse (laʿn).
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Distance from evil is tasbih; distance from good is a curse (laʿn).

positions.position: Ahl al-tadhkir also take tasbih as expressing wonder: at subduing powerful animals for humans, creating without fatigue, teaching without a human teacher, and forgiving long sin after brief repentance.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (أهل التذكير): Ahl al-tadhkir also take tasbih as expressing wonder: at subduing powerful animals for humans, creating without fatigue, teaching without a human teacher, and forgiving long sin after brief repentance.

positions.position: Talha b. ʿUbayd Allah asked the Prophet what subhan Allah means; the Prophet explained it as declaring God free of every evil.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL (طلحة بن عبيد الله): Talha b. ʿUbayd Allah asked the Prophet what subhan Allah means; the Prophet explained it as declaring God free of every evil.

positions.position: Both tasbīḥ and taqdīs declare God far removed from imperfection; the terms evoke traveling far through land or water. Taqdīs also means purification, since cleansing removes impurity.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI-FULL (author): Both tasbīḥ and taqdīs declare God far removed from imperfection; the terms evoke traveling far through land or water. Taqdīs also means purification, since cleansing removes impurity.

positions.position: An alternative makes the bāʾ causal and attaches it to تسبيح; Ibn ʿAṭiyya treats the phrase as an interpolated acknowledgment of God's guidance.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (author): An alternative makes the bāʾ causal and attaches it to تسبيح; Ibn ʿAṭiyya treats the phrase as an interpolated acknowledgment of God's guidance.

positions.position: Tasbih literally means declaring God far removed; here it means declaring Him free of whatever is unbefitting, and it takes a direct object or a lām-marked object.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Tasbih literally means declaring God far removed; here it means declaring Him free of whatever is unbefitting, and it takes a direct object or a lām-marked object.

positions.position: The omitted object of tasbih may be construed with the lām, following the parallel construction, or without it, following the verb's basic transitivity.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): The omitted object of tasbih may be construed with the lām, following the parallel construction, or without it, following the verb's basic transitivity.

positions.position: Angels glorify God by attributing blessings to Him and praising Him.
positions.reasons: JISHUMI (author): Angels glorify God by attributing blessings to Him and praising Him.

positions.position: A second explanation takes tasbih as prayer, as in 37:143 where Jonah is called one of the worshippers.
positions.reasons: TABRISI (ابن عباس وابن مسعود): A second explanation takes tasbih as prayer, as in 37:143 where Jonah is called one of the worshippers.

positions.position: One interpretation takes the angels’ tasbīḥ to mean prayer.
positions.reasons: IBNJAWZI-ZAD (ابن مسعود وابن عباس): One interpretation takes the angels’ tasbīḥ to mean prayer.

positions.position: There is no need to reorder the phrase as though bi-ḥamdika interrupts wa-nuqaddisu; word order inversion is limited to poetic necessity, and praise naturally accompanies tasbīḥ.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): There is no need to reorder the phrase as though bi-ḥamdika interrupts wa-nuqaddisu; word order inversion is limited to poetic necessity, and praise naturally accompanies tasbīḥ.
