question: What formulas and practices of angelic praise are reported?

positions.position: Al-Hasan says the angels say Subhan Allah wa bihamdihi; this is the prayer of creation, beasts, and other creatures besides humans, by which they receive provision.
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI-FULL (الحسن): Al-Hasan says the angels say Subhan Allah wa bihamdihi; this is the prayer of creation, beasts, and other creatures besides humans, by which they receive provision.

positions.position: Abu Dharr reports that the Prophet named Subhan Allah wa bihamdihi as the best speech chosen by God for His angels or servants; Baghawi gives no grading.
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI-FULL (أبو ذر): Abu Dharr reports that the Prophet named Subhan Allah wa bihamdihi as the best speech chosen by God for His angels or servants; Baghawi gives no grading.

positions.position: ʿAbd al-Rahman b. Qurt reports that on the night of the Night Journey the Prophet heard glorification in the highest heavens: subhan al-ʿAli al-Aʿla; al-Bayhaqi reports it.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL (عبد الرحمن بن قرط): ʿAbd al-Rahman b. Qurt reports that on the night of the Night Journey the Prophet heard glorification in the highest heavens: subhan al-ʿAli al-Aʿla; al-Bayhaqi reports it.

positions.position: Mujāhid interprets tasbīḥ as magnifying God; other views make it a special angelic liturgy or the formula subḥān Allāh wa-bi-ḥamdih.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (مجاهد): Mujāhid interprets tasbīḥ as magnifying God; other views make it a special angelic liturgy or the formula subḥān Allāh wa-bi-ḥamdih.

positions.position: In a report from ʿUbāda ibn al-Ṣāmit through Abū Dharr, the Prophet says the best words are what God chose for angels or servants: subḥān Allāh wa-bi-ḥamdih.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (النبي): In a report from ʿUbāda ibn al-Ṣāmit through Abū Dharr, the Prophet says the best words are what God chose for angels or servants: subḥān Allāh wa-bi-ḥamdih.

positions.position: Al-Rāghib reads سبحان من علقمة sarcastically as سبحان علقمة with من added; another explanation supplies الله من أجل علقمة, which al-Samīn questions as applying the formula to other than God.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (الراغب): Al-Rāghib reads سبحان من علقمة sarcastically as سبحان علقمة with من added; another explanation supplies الله من أجل علقمة, which al-Samīn questions as applying the formula to other than God.

positions.position: In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet answers that the best speech is what God chose for His angels: Subhan Allah wa bihamdihi.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR-FULL (رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم عن أبي ذر): In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet answers that the best speech is what God chose for His angels: Subhan Allah wa bihamdihi.

positions.position: Al-Bayhaqi reports that during the Night Journey the Prophet heard glorification in the highest heavens: Subhan al-Ali al-Ala, subhanahu wa taala.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR-FULL (عبد الرحمن بن قرط عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم): Al-Bayhaqi reports that during the Night Journey the Prophet heard glorification in the highest heavens: Subhan al-Ali al-Ala, subhanahu wa taala.

positions.position: Tasbih may denote the specific formula “Glory to the Possessor of sovereignty and dominion, glory to the Possessor of might and power, glory to the Living who never dies.”
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (قيل): Tasbih may denote the specific formula “Glory to the Possessor of sovereignty and dominion, glory to the Possessor of might and power, glory to the Living who never dies.”

question: How does “with Your praise” work and what does it mean?

positions.position: بحمدك is circumstantial: they glorify God while praising Him and joined to His praise.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF-FULL (author): بحمدك is circumstantial: they glorify God while praising Him and joined to His praise.

positions.position: Bi-hamdika can mean joining praise to glorification; alternatively, it is an interjection: “we glorify and sanctify,” then a submission that God is praised for guiding them to this.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): Bi-hamdika can mean joining praise to glorification; alternatively, it is an interjection: “we glorify and sanctify,” then a submission that God is praised for guiding them to this.

positions.position: Al-Kashshaf treats ‘with your praise’ as a circumstantial phrase: we glorify you while praising you and clothed in your praise.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (صاحب الكشاف): Al-Kashshaf treats ‘with your praise’ as a circumstantial phrase: we glorify you while praising you and clothed in your praise.

positions.position: Bi-hamdika may mean that the angels join praise to tasbih; al-hamd means praise.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL (author): Bi-hamdika may mean that the angels join praise to tasbih; al-hamd means praise.

positions.position: Alternatively, bi-hamdika is a parenthetical acknowledgment: the angels say they glorify and sanctify, while affirming that God is praised for guiding them to this worship.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL (author): Alternatively, bi-hamdika is a parenthetical acknowledgment: the angels say they glorify and sanctify, while affirming that God is praised for guiding them to this worship.

positions.position: Qatada takes tasbih in its ordinary linguistic sense, saying subhan Allah; al-Qurtubi calls this correct and cites the Prophet's report that subhan Allah wa bi-hamdih is among God's chosen words.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL (قتادة): Qatada takes tasbih in its ordinary linguistic sense, saying subhan Allah; al-Qurtubi calls this correct and cites the Prophet's report that subhan Allah wa bi-hamdih is among God's chosen words.

positions.position: Abu Dharr reports that the Prophet was asked which speech is best and replied that it is what God chose for His angels or servants: subhan Allah wa bi-hamdih; Muslim transmits it.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL (أبو ذر): Abu Dharr reports that the Prophet was asked which speech is best and replied that it is what God chose for His angels or servants: subhan Allah wa bi-hamdih; Muslim transmits it.

positions.position: بحمدك is circumstantial: ‘while praising You for teaching us to know You and enabling our glorification’; this qualification prevents the angels’ self-attribution of praise from implying conceit.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI-FULL (author): بحمدك is circumstantial: ‘while praising You for teaching us to know You and enabling our glorification’; this qualification prevents the angels’ self-attribution of praise from implying conceit.

positions.position: Alternatively, bāʾ marks cause: praise arises from enabling and beneficence, so the angels glorify because God grants them good; ḥamd is annexed to its object.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): Alternatively, bāʾ marks cause: praise arises from enabling and beneficence, so the angels glorify because God grants them good; ḥamd is annexed to its object.

positions.position: الحمد is a verbal noun annexed to its object, with subject omitted as بحمدنا إياك; the claim that the noun itself contains a subject is mistaken.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (author): الحمد is a verbal noun annexed to its object, with subject omitted as بحمدنا إياك; the claim that the noun itself contains a subject is mistaken.

positions.position: بحمدك attaches to an omitted circumstantial phrase: they glorify accompanied by praise, two nested circumstantial states.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (author): بحمدك attaches to an omitted circumstantial phrase: they glorify accompanied by praise, two nested circumstantial states.

positions.position: The phrase “with Your praise” is circumstantial; the bāʾ denotes continued companionship and accompaniment.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): The phrase “with Your praise” is circumstantial; the bāʾ denotes continued companionship and accompaniment.

positions.position: The bāʾ marks accompaniment: the angels glorify God with praise, since their utterance includes praise and exaltation, avoiding strained analyses of the phrase.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR-FULL (author): The bāʾ marks accompaniment: the angels glorify God with praise, since their utterance includes praise and exaltation, avoiding strained analyses of the phrase.

positions.position: An alternate rendering is We glorify Thee while praising Thee.
positions.reasons: STUDYQURAN (Z): An alternate rendering is We glorify Thee while praising Thee.

question: What does the angels' taqdīs mean?

positions.position: The angels ascribe purity and holiness to God
positions.reasons: MUQATIL (author): God prayed mercy upon Adam's first praise and said he was created for glorification and sanctification. TAB-FULL (author): Al-Tabari defines taqdis as purification and magnification: subbuh denotes declaring God free of defects, quddus his purity and exaltation, and holy land is purified land. TAB-FULL (أبو صالح): Abu Salih interprets taqdis as magnifying and glorifying God. TAB-FULL (مجاهد): Mujahid says taqdis means to magnify and exalt God. SULAMI (الواسطي): After the angels boasted of praise and sanctification, God taught Adam the names, making them recognize their own shortfall and confess ignorance. SULAMI (أبو عثمان المغربي): The angels' claim to praise and sanctify God exemplifies how creaturely claims lead to ignorance. WAHIDI-BASIT (author): Naqdis means to purify and declare God free of any unbefitting deficiency; taqdis and quds mean purification, and bayt al-maqdis is the purified house. JISHUMI (author): Another account treats the lām as extra and the sanctification as directed to God Himself. IBNATIYYA-FULL (مجاهد): Mujāhid, Abū Ṣāliḥ, and others explain “we sanctify You” as magnifying God and declaring His remembrance free of anything unworthy. TABRISI (سيبويه): سبحان means God's release from every evil and His sanctification; Sibawayh treats it as a fixed proper name, and poets use tanwin by necessity. QURTUBI-FULL (مجاهد): Mujahid, Abu Salih, and others say taqdis means magnifying God and purifying His mention of what heretics attribute to Him. QURTUBI-FULL (أرباب المعاني): They say God addressed angels not for counsel but to elicit their view of action, worship, praise, and sanctification, then restored their rank by ordering prostration to Adam. SAMIN-DURR (author): Al-Samīn takes Ibn ʿAṭiyya to aim at a causal bāʾ with an omitted verb: praise of God occasioned their glorification and sanctification. IBNKATHIR-FULL (ابن جرير): Ibn Jarir defines taqdis as glorification and purification: subbuh denotes declaring God free of defect and quddus denotes His purity and exaltedness; the angels disavow what polytheists attribute to Him and affirm His purity from impure qualities. BURSEVI (author): The lām in “for You” may explain the act, as in a supplication formula, or be an added particle; the implied object is sanctifying God. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): Taqdīs may also be an act of belief; the hadith lā quddisat umma means God has not purified a community from satanic impurities when its weak cannot claim rights. TABATABAI (author): God does not deny that the earthly successor will cause corruption and bloodshed, nor does He dispute the angels' own glorification and sanctification.

positions.position: The angels purify themselves or their deeds for God
positions.reasons: SULAMI (الواسطي): Glorification and sanctification do not themselves bring one near to God; nearness comes through pre-eternal grace, which sins cannot diminish. WAHIDI-BASIT (أبو إسحاق): Abu Ishaq reads the lām as purposive: the angels purify themselves for God, cleansing their hearts of idolatry and bodies of disobedience; bayt al-maqdis is the purified house or place where one is purified of sins. JISHUMI (أبو مسلم): Abū Muslim takes the angels’ sanctification as purifying themselves from sins for God’s sake and pleasure. IBNATIYYA-FULL (الضحاك): Al-Dahhak and others explain “we sanctify for You” as purifying themselves to seek God’s approval; sanctification means purification. QURTUBI-FULL (الضحاك): Al-Dahhak and others interpret taqdis as purifying themselves for God in pursuit of His pleasure. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (الضحاك): Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and others interpret taqdīs as purifying themselves for God from impurities; Abū Muslim instead makes its object their deeds, purified from sins. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (قول غير مسمى): One proposed explanation is that God knew the angels were magnifying themselves through their glorification and sanctification. IBNKATHIR-FULL (قيل): Another explanation takes God's reply as pointing to Iblis's presence among the angels, despite their description of themselves as glorifying and sanctifying God. ALUSI-FULL (author): Taqdis may also mean purification: the angels purify themselves from impurities, their acts from sins, or their hearts from attending to anything besides God.

positions.position: Taqdīs means prayer
positions.reasons: ABDURRAZZAQ (author): Qatada glosses taqdis as prayer. TAB-FULL (قتادة): Qatada says the angels’ taqdis means prayer. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (مجاهد وأبو صالح): Mujāhid and Abū Ṣāliḥ understand taqdīs as magnifying and glorifying God; other reports interpret it as prayer or purification from human deeds.

positions.position: Angels purify their deeds for God
positions.reasons: SULAMI (جعفر): When the angels boasted of their deeds, glorification, and sanctification, God struck them with ignorance until they confessed they had no knowledge. THALABI (بعض العلماء): Some scholars reorder the sense as “we glorify and sanctify You by Your praise”: otherwise the angels seem to boast of their deeds, whereas this credits every act of worship to God.

positions.position: Quddus follows fa'ul from quds, purity.
positions.reasons: IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB (author): Quddus follows fa'ul from quds, purity.

positions.position: Hazirat al-Quds is Paradise, free of excrement, urine and menstruation.
positions.reasons: IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB (author): Hazirat al-Quds is Paradise, free of excrement, urine and menstruation.

positions.position: Al-Dahhak glosses taqdis as purification.
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (الضحاك): Al-Dahhak glosses taqdis as purification.

positions.position: One interpretation of the angels’ taqdīs is that they pray.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI-FULL (author): One interpretation of the angels’ taqdīs is that they pray.

positions.position: Another analysis treats the lām as expressing purpose: we sanctify for Your sake and pleasure.
positions.reasons: JISHUMI (author): Another analysis treats the lām as expressing purpose: we sanctify for Your sake and pleasure.

positions.position: The root means purification, as in “the holy land,” Bayt al-Maqdis, and al-Quds, the thing used to purify.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): The root means purification, as in “the holy land,” Bayt al-Maqdis, and al-Quds, the thing used to purify.

positions.position: تقديس means purification, opposed to defilement; القدس can also mean a vessel for washing.
positions.reasons: TABRISI (author): تقديس means purification, opposed to defilement; القدس can also mean a vessel for washing.

positions.position: Quds means purity.
positions.reasons: IBNJAWZI-ZAD (author): Quds means purity.

positions.position: Taqdis means purification, as in the expression ‘the Holy Land.’
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Taqdis means purification, as in the expression ‘the Holy Land.’

positions.position: ʿAisha reports that the Prophet said in bowing and prostration, subbuh quddus, Lord of the angels and the Spirit; Muslim transmits it.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL (عائشة): ʿAisha reports that the Prophet said in bowing and prostration, subbuh quddus, Lord of the angels and the Spirit; Muslim transmits it.

positions.position: Across its forms, quds means purification: the Holy Land is purified, al-Malik al-Quddus is the Pure, and the sacred valley is purified; Bayt al-Maqdis names a place of purification from sins.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL (author): Across its forms, quds means purification: the Holy Land is purified, al-Malik al-Quddus is the Pure, and the sacred valley is purified; Bayt al-Maqdis names a place of purification from sins.

positions.position: Glorification denies partner, incapacity, and defect; sanctification also denies attachment, passivity, contingency, multiplicity, and potentiality, so every sanctified being glorifies but not vice versa.
positions.reasons: QASHANI (author): Glorification denies partner, incapacity, and defect; sanctification also denies attachment, passivity, contingency, multiplicity, and potentiality, so every sanctified being glorifies but not vice versa.

positions.position: The nearest angels, pure spirits, are sanctifiers because they are un-veiled, overcome lower realms with light, act on others, and possess all perfections actually; other angels glorify.
positions.reasons: QASHANI (author): The nearest angels, pure spirits, are sanctifiers because they are un-veiled, overcome lower realms with light, act on others, and possess all perfections actually; other angels glorify.

positions.position: Angels purify their hearts for God
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): Another spiritual interpretation takes taqdīs as cleansing hearts from attention to anything besides God.

positions.position: تقديس means purification, as in الأرض المقدسة, بيت المقدس, and روح القدس.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (author): تقديس means purification, as in الأرض المقدسة, بيت المقدس, and روح القدس.

positions.position: Al-Dahhak explains taqdis as purification.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR-FULL (الضحاك): Al-Dahhak explains taqdis as purification.

positions.position: The angels' wording pairs corruption with glorification and bloodshed with sanctification: glorification supports reform, while sanctification protects blood; the latter is nobler.
positions.reasons: BURHAN (author): The angels' wording pairs corruption with glorification and bloodshed with sanctification: glorification supports reform, while sanctification protects blood; the latter is nobler.

positions.position: Ibn Masud and some Companions gloss the angels' “we sanctify You” as “we pray to You.”
positions.reasons: DURR-FULL (ابن مسعود): Ibn Masud and some Companions gloss the angels' “we sanctify You” as “we pray to You.”

positions.position: Ibn Abbas says taqdis means purification.
positions.reasons: DURR-FULL (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas says taqdis means purification.

positions.position: Angels vary in form and size; only people with sanctified souls see them in their true forms, though they may appear in bodies visible to all.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Angels vary in form and size; only people with sanctified souls see them in their true forms, though they may appear in bodies visible to all.

positions.position: Taqdīs means declaring free of deficiency and purifying; it can be enacted in practice, as the word muqaddas in Imruʾ al-Qays's verse suggests.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR-FULL (author): Taqdīs means declaring free of deficiency and purifying; it can be enacted in practice, as the word muqaddas in Imruʾ al-Qays's verse suggests.

positions.position: Another interpretation is that they purify God from impurities.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI-FULL (author): Another interpretation is that they purify God from impurities.

positions.position: They declare God transcendent above whatever is unbefitting Him.
positions.reasons: WAHIDI-WAJIZ (author): They declare God transcendent above whatever is unbefitting Him.

positions.position: One interpretation is that the angels declare God transcendent above bodily attributes and purify Him of reprehensible acts.
positions.reasons: JISHUMI (author): One interpretation is that the angels declare God transcendent above bodily attributes and purify Him of reprehensible acts.

positions.position: Qaddas means to praise God as holy and pure; other explanations are to purify themselves for obedience or to declare Him transcendent.
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI-FULL (author): Qaddas means to praise God as holy and pure; other explanations are to purify themselves for obedience or to declare Him transcendent.

positions.position: Some interpret “we sanctify You” as “we pray to You”; Ibn ʿAṭiyya judges this weak.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL (قوم): Some interpret “we sanctify You” as “we pray to You”; Ibn ʿAṭiyya judges this weak.

turns_on: Whether taqdīs purifies God in speech or the angels and their deeds.

question: What is the force of “for You” after nuqaddisu?

positions.position: Nuqaddisuka and nuqaddisu laka have the same meaning, like forms of nusabbih.
positions.reasons: IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB (author): Nuqaddisuka and nuqaddisu laka have the same meaning, like forms of nusabbih.

positions.position: Al-Tabari says ونقدسك could replace ونقدس لك with no change in meaning; both transitive constructions are idiomatic, as Qur’anic usage also shows.
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (author): Al-Tabari says ونقدسك could replace ونقدس لك with no change in meaning; both transitive constructions are idiomatic, as Qur’anic usage also shows.

positions.position: Nuqaddisu laka means purifying ourselves for God; the obedient person is purified, and Bayt al-Maqdis is the purified house or place of purification from sins.
positions.reasons: ZAJJAJ (author): Nuqaddisu laka means purifying ourselves for God; the obedient person is purified, and Bayt al-Maqdis is the purified house or place of purification from sins.

positions.position: When a consonant precedes the suffix yāʾ, speakers agree on fatḥa in examples such as بشراي and غلاماي, supporting that as its underlying vowel after a vowel too.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA (author): When a consonant precedes the suffix yāʾ, speakers agree on fatḥa in examples such as بشراي and غلاماي, supporting that as its underlying vowel after a vowel too.

positions.position: Nuqaddisu means declaring God transcendent; on one analysis the lām is merely connective.
positions.reasons: THALABI (author): Nuqaddisu means declaring God transcendent; on one analysis the lām is merely connective.

positions.position: The Hudhaylī line using ألكني is cited as evidence for the sense “send me.”
positions.reasons: MAWARDI-FULL (author): The Hudhaylī line using ألكني is cited as evidence for the sense “send me.”

positions.position: Abu Ali al-Farisi says the angels declare God free of evil and refuse to attribute evil to Him; the lām is not purposive but functions like that in 27:72. He also analyzes al-muqaddas as either a
positions.reasons: WAHIDI-BASIT (أبو علي الفارسي): Abu Ali al-Farisi says the angels declare God free of evil and refuse to attribute evil to Him; the lām is not purposive but functions like that in 27:72. He also analyzes al-muqaddas as either a verbal noun or a place, with bayt al-maqdis a place of purification cleansed of idols, as in 2:125.

positions.position: One analysis treats the lām as extra and reads the phrase as nuqaddisuka, we sanctify You.
positions.reasons: JISHUMI (author): One analysis treats the lām as extra and reads the phrase as nuqaddisuka, we sanctify You.

positions.position: The lām is an added connective particle.
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI-FULL (author): The lām is an added connective particle.

positions.position: One explanation is declaring God free of deficient attributes and unworthy things; on this reading the lām is extra.
positions.reasons: TABRISI (author): One explanation is declaring God free of deficient attributes and unworthy things; on this reading the lām is extra.

positions.position: Some Arabs keep the hamza, but most shift its vowel to the lām and drop it, saying ملك.
positions.reasons: TABRISI (author): Some Arabs keep the hamza, but most shift its vowel to the lām and drop it, saying ملك.

positions.position: Some hold that the lām in لك is extra.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI-FULL (قيل): Some hold that the lām in لك is extra.

positions.position: نقدس لك means purifying ourselves for God; alternatively tasbih and taqdis mean declaring God free of evil, with a root sense of going away and distancing.
positions.reasons: NASAFI-FULL (author): نقدس لك means purifying ourselves for God; alternatively tasbih and taqdis mean declaring God free of evil, with a root sense of going away and distancing.

positions.position: The lām in laka may be extra, purposive, attached to nuqaddisu or nusabbiḥu, transitive, or explanatory with an omitted taqdīsuna laka; Abū Ḥayyān prefers the transitive function.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): The lām in laka may be extra, purposive, attached to nuqaddisu or nusabbiḥu, transitive, or explanatory with an omitted taqdīsuna laka; Abū Ḥayyān prefers the transitive function.

positions.position: Wa-nuqaddisu laka reinforces wa-nusabbiḥu because purification and declaring God free of evil are close in meaning.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): Wa-nuqaddisu laka reinforces wa-nusabbiḥu because purification and declaring God free of evil are close in meaning.

positions.position: لك may attach to نقدس or نسبح with a causal sense; it may also be redundant (a weak view), transitive, or explanatory as in سقيا لك.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (author): لك may attach to نقدس or نسبح with a causal sense; it may also be redundant (a weak view), transitive, or explanatory as in سقيا لك.

positions.position: The estimate تقديسنا لك suits the context better than estimating أعني.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (author): The estimate تقديسنا لك suits the context better than estimating أعني.

positions.position: Although qaddasa is transitive directly, the lām with its object intensifies the action, as in shakarta laka and naṣaḥtu laka; Arabic usage treats this as eloquent emphasis.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR-FULL (author): Although qaddasa is transitive directly, the lām with its object intensifies the action, as in shakarta laka and naṣaḥtu laka; Arabic usage treats this as eloquent emphasis.

positions.position: Alternatively, the lām marks purpose: the angels purify their hearts of associating partners with God and their bodies of disobedience for His sake.
positions.reasons: THALABI (author): Alternatively, the lām marks purpose: the angels purify their hearts of associating partners with God and their bodies of disobedience for His sake.

positions.position: The author rejects analyses that attach laka to an omitted word or make it mean for your sake with an omitted object, calling these departures from eloquent usage; an explanatory lām remains possible.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR-FULL (author): The author rejects analyses that attach laka to an omitted word or make it mean for your sake with an omitted object, calling these departures from eloquent usage; an explanatory lām remains possible.

question: How are tasbīḥ and taqdīs related?

positions.position: The angels’ tasbih clears God of what polytheists attribute to him and includes prayer; taqdis ascribes purity to him, free from what disbelievers allege.
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (author): The angels’ tasbih clears God of what polytheists attribute to him and includes prayer; taqdis ascribes purity to him, free from what disbelievers allege.

positions.position: Tasbih is declaring God free of evil and unworthy attributes; السبوح deserves glorification and القدوس purification and sanctification.
positions.reasons: TABRISI (author): Tasbih is declaring God free of evil and unworthy attributes; السبوح deserves glorification and القدوس purification and sanctification.

positions.position: A group including Qatada says taqdis means prayer. Ibn ʿAtiyya calls this weak, but al-Qurtubi says it is sound because prayer includes magnification, sanctification, and tasbih.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL (قتادة): A group including Qatada says taqdis means prayer. Ibn ʿAtiyya calls this weak, but al-Qurtubi says it is sound because prayer includes magnification, sanctification, and tasbih.

positions.position: Qatada glosses tasbih as tasbih itself and taqdis as prayer.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR-FULL (قتادة): Qatada glosses tasbih as tasbih itself and taqdis as prayer.

positions.position: Qatada explains the angels' tasbih as glorification and their taqdis as prayer.
positions.reasons: DURR-FULL (قتادة): Qatada explains the angels' tasbih as glorification and their taqdis as prayer.

positions.position: Tasbih declares God free of what is unfitting; praise recalls His blessings; taqdis describes Him with fitting exaltation and denies what is unfitting.
positions.reasons: BURSEVI (author): Tasbih declares God free of what is unfitting; praise recalls His blessings; taqdis describes Him with fitting exaltation and denies what is unfitting.

positions.position: Al-Taysir distinguishes tasbih as negating what is unfitting for God and taqdis as affirming what is fitting for Him.
positions.reasons: BURSEVI (التيسير): Al-Taysir distinguishes tasbih as negating what is unfitting for God and taqdis as affirming what is fitting for Him.

positions.position: Dawud al-Qaysari says tasbih is broader: taqdis also negates perfections ascribed to created things, since their attachment to creation restricts them.
positions.reasons: BURSEVI (داود القيصري): Dawud al-Qaysari says tasbih is broader: taqdis also negates perfections ascribed to created things, since their attachment to creation restricts them.

positions.position: Taqdis is commonly treated as synonymous with tasbih.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Taqdis is commonly treated as synonymous with tasbih.

positions.position: To avoid redundancy, one view assigns tasbih to deeds and taqdis to beliefs.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (قيل): To avoid redundancy, one view assigns tasbih to deeds and taqdis to beliefs.

positions.position: Another view makes tasbih transcendence from what is unbefitting and taqdis a stronger transcendence of God's essence from what He does not deem fitting; the pairing “سبوح قدوس” supports this.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (قيل): Another view makes tasbih transcendence from what is unbefitting and taqdis a stronger transcendence of God's essence from what He does not deem fitting; the pairing “سبوح قدوس” supports this.

question: How is “I know what” parsed?

positions.position: «أعلم» can be a present verb or a participle meaning “knowing,” as «الله أكبر» can mean “God is great.”
positions.reasons: NAHHAS (author): «أعلم» can be a present verb or a participle meaning “knowing,” as «الله أكبر» can mean “God is great.”

positions.position: For “I know what you do not know,” the more apparent parsing makes aʿlam a future verb and mā its direct object.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): For “I know what you do not know,” the more apparent parsing makes aʿlam a future verb and mā its direct object.

positions.position: An alternative parses aʿlam as a noun with mā in the genitive as its complement.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL (قوم): An alternative parses aʿlam as a noun with mā in the genitive as its complement.

positions.position: Sībawayh and al-Khalīl say an afʿal form used as an indefinite proper name does not take nunation; al-Akhfash allows it.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL (سيبويه والخليل): Sībawayh and al-Khalīl say an afʿal form used as an indefinite proper name does not take nunation; al-Akhfash allows it.

positions.position: ما is a relative pronoun with an omitted object pronoun understood as لا تعلمونه; the clause is the accusative object of أعلم.
positions.reasons: TABRISI (author): ما is a relative pronoun with an omitted object pronoun understood as لا تعلمونه; the clause is the accusative object of أعلم.

positions.position: Aʿlam may be a future verb or an adjective meaning knowing, as in Allahu akbar meaning great; in the first reading ma is its accusative object, in the second it is genitive by annexation.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL (author): Aʿlam may be a future verb or an adjective meaning knowing, as in Allahu akbar meaning great; in the first reading ma is its accusative object, in the second it is genitive by annexation.

positions.position: Ibn ʿAtiyya says aʿlam cannot take nunation here by grammarians' agreement; Sibawayh and al-Khalil do not nunate an indefinite proper name on the afʿal pattern, while al-Akhfash does.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL (ابن عطية): Ibn ʿAtiyya says aʿlam cannot take nunation here by grammarians' agreement; Sibawayh and al-Khalil do not nunate an indefinite proper name on the afʿal pattern, while al-Akhfash does.

positions.position: Al-Mahdawi allows an assumed tanwin on aʿlam if it means ʿalim, with ma then accusative, analogous to the construction hajjaj bayt Allah.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL (المهدوي): Al-Mahdawi allows an assumed tanwin on aʿlam if it means ʿalim, with ma then accusative, analogous to the construction hajjaj bayt Allah.

positions.position: ما is a relative pronoun and object of أعلم, with its antecedent omitted.
positions.reasons: NASAFI-FULL (author): ما is a relative pronoun and object of أعلم, with its antecedent omitted.

positions.position: He prefers parsing ما after أعلم as a relative pronoun and rejects treating it as an indefinite adjective.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): He prefers parsing ما after أعلم as a relative pronoun and rejects treating it as an indefinite adjective.

positions.position: Makkī, al-Mahdawī, and others allow أعلم as an active participle; on that parse ما may be genitive by annexation or accusative.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (مكي بن أبي طالب والمهدوي وغيرهما): Makkī, al-Mahdawī, and others allow أعلم as an active participle; on that parse ما may be genitive by annexation or accusative.

positions.position: Others parse أعلم as a comparative meaning more knowing than you, with ما governed as the object of an implied verb meaning I know.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (بعضهم): Others parse أعلم as a comparative meaning more knowing than you, with ما governed as the object of an implied verb meaning I know.

positions.position: The clause إني أعلم ما لا تعلمون occupies the accusative position as content of قال.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (author): The clause إني أعلم ما لا تعلمون occupies the accusative position as content of قال.

positions.position: أعلم is apparently an imperfect verb governing ما as object; ما may be relative or indefinite with the resumptive pronoun omitted.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (author): أعلم is apparently an imperfect verb governing ما as object; ما may be relative or indefinite with the resumptive pronoun omitted.

positions.position: Al-Mahdawī, Makkī, and Abū al-Baqāʾ treat أعلم as the noun عالم; ما may be genitive or accusative and أعلم is diptote.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (المهدوي): Al-Mahdawī, Makkī, and Abū al-Baqāʾ treat أعلم as the noun عالم; ما may be genitive or accusative and أعلم is diptote.

positions.position: Another analysis takes أعلم as comparative with منكم omitted and ما as object of implied علمت, since the comparative does not govern it.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (author): Another analysis takes أعلم as comparative with منكم omitted and ما as object of implied علمت, since the comparative does not govern it.

positions.position: Ma is declarative or relative before laysa, lam, or la, and after illa, as in the cited examples.
positions.reasons: BURHAN (author): Ma is declarative or relative before laysa, lam, or la, and after illa, as in the cited examples.

question: What does God know that the angels do not?

positions.position: God knew righteous people would arise from Adam's descendants
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (قتادة): Qatada says God knew that Adam's descendants would include prophets, messengers, righteous people, and inhabitants of Paradise. JISHUMI (author): One explanation is that God knows prophets, scholars, and saints will arise among Adam’s descendants and knows their great work in religion and worldly affairs. TABRISI (قتادة): Qatada says God knows which prophets and righteous people will descend from Adam. IBNJAWZI-ZAD (قتادة): Qatāda says God knows that prophets and righteous people will emerge from Adam’s descendants. IBNJAWZI-ZAD (الزجاج): Al-Zajjāj says God knows how events end: testing may lead someone thought obedient, like Iblīs, to sin, while someone thought sinful may obey. QURTUBI-FULL (قتادة): Qatada says God's hidden knowledge was that among those to be created on earth would be prophets, virtuous people, and the obedient. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (قتادة): Qatāda says God knew that prophets and righteous people would descend from the vicegerent. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (الزجاج): Al-Zajjāj says God knows outcomes: trials may lead someone thought obedient into sin, or someone thought sinful into obedience.

positions.position: God knew Iblis's hidden pride and coming disobedience
positions.reasons: MUJAHID (author): God knew Iblis's disobedience and created him for it. TAB-FULL (مجاهد): Mujahid says God knew Iblis's disobedience and that He created him for it. TAB-FULL (مجاهد): Mujahid says God knew Iblis's disobedience and created him for it, while knowing Adam's obedience and creating him for it. IBNABIHATIM (ابن عباس): A report from Ibn Abbas says Iblis led the angels of the lowest heaven, then became proud and rebellious; God knew the rebelliousness within Iblis. Al-Suddi is also reported similarly. IBNABIHATIM (مجاهد): Mujahid says God knew Iblis's disobedience and created him for it. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (ابن عباس ومجاهد والسدي عن أشياخه): Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and al-Suddī from his teachers say God knew what was in Iblis’s mind despite his rebellion and disobedience. ALUSI-FULL (قيل): One explanation is that God knows Iblis's coming disobedience and Adam's obedience. TAB-FULL (ابن مسعود، وأصحاب النبي): Al-Tabari transmits from Ibn Masud and other Companions the gloss that God's knowledge concerned Iblis's affair. TAB-FULL (مجاهد): Mujahid once glosses the phrase as God's knowledge of Iblis's created-for disobedience, and once as referring to Adam.

positions.position: God's knowledge encompasses unseen realities
positions.reasons: SAMARRAI-ASRAR (author): The verse before the story summarizes both Adam's narrative and the two requirements of vicegerency: the earth is given to people and God knows everything. STUDYQURAN (R): The phrase generally means that good will come from humanity despite inevitable bloodshed and corruption, but only God knows what that good is.

positions.position: God knew His mercy and forgiveness for humans
positions.reasons: THALABI (author): Another explanation is that God knows humans will sin and that He will forgive them.

positions.position: God knew the hidden wisdom and benefits of the appointment
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF-FULL (author): God knows benefits and wise purposes hidden from the angels.

positions.position: God knows the believers’ pure beliefs and keen inward protection of their covenantal love, even when disobedience stains their outward state.
positions.reasons: QUSHAYRI (author): God knows the believers’ pure beliefs and keen inward protection of their covenantal love, even when disobedience stains their outward state.

positions.position: God knows His love for them and the inward secrets He hides in them, unlike angels who openly display their states.
positions.reasons: QUSHAYRI (author): God knows His love for them and the inward secrets He hides in them, unlike angels who openly display their states.

positions.position: Qatada says God knew Adam’s descendants would include people who obey Him.
positions.reasons: WAHIDI-BASIT (قتادة): Qatada says God knew Adam’s descendants would include people who obey Him.

positions.position: A further estimate is that God knew their states when He spoke to the angels.
positions.reasons: JISHUMI (author): A further estimate is that God knew their states when He spoke to the angels.

positions.position: Creating people whom God knows will disbelieve can still be wise and right.
positions.reasons: JISHUMI (author): Creating people whom God knows will disbelieve can still be wise and right.

positions.position: On Ibn ʿAbbās’s account, God’s “I know what you do not know” refers to the discordant pride hidden within Iblīs, unknown to the angels.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL (ابن عباس): On Ibn ʿAbbās’s account, God’s “I know what you do not know” refers to the discordant pride hidden within Iblīs, unknown to the angels.

positions.position: God knew Iblīs harbored pride and disobedience and wished to reveal it to the angels; this is related from Ibn ʿAbbās and by al-Suddī from his elders.
positions.reasons: IBNJAWZI-ZAD (ابن عباس والسدي عن أشياخه): God knew Iblīs harbored pride and disobedience and wished to reveal it to the angels; this is related from Ibn ʿAbbās and by al-Suddī from his elders.

positions.position: One interpretation is that God knows the pride and disobedience within Iblīs; this is attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and al-Suddī from his elders.
positions.reasons: IBNJAWZI-ZAD (ابن عباس ومجاهد والسدي عن أشياخه): One interpretation is that God knows the pride and disobedience within Iblīs; this is attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and al-Suddī from his elders.

positions.position: Ibn Zayd takes the words to mean that God knows He will fill Hell with jinn and humans.
positions.reasons: IBNJAWZI-ZAD (ابن زيد): Ibn Zayd takes the words to mean that God knows He will fill Hell with jinn and humans.

positions.position: On al-Qaffal's reading, God knows humanity's hidden virtues and reasons for creating them, beyond their outward corruption.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (القفال): On al-Qaffal's reading, God knows humanity's hidden virtues and reasons for creating them, beyond their outward corruption.

positions.position: Ibn Zayd says God knew which jinn and humans would fill Hell.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (ابن زيد): Ibn Zayd says God knew which jinn and humans would fill Hell.

positions.position: The wording leaves unspecified what God knows beyond the angels’ knowledge; that claim requires their submission and acceptance of his decision because his knowledge encompasses what no scholar can encompass.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): The wording leaves unspecified what God knows beyond the angels’ knowledge; that claim requires their submission and acceptance of his decision because his knowledge encompasses what no scholar can encompass.

positions.position: The human capacity for the hidden of the hidden is the concealed secret in human preparedness that God knows and the angels do not.
positions.reasons: BURSEVI (author): The human capacity for the hidden of the hidden is the concealed secret in human preparedness that God knows and the angels do not.

positions.position: God knew Adam's knowledge and fitness
positions.reasons: BURSEVI (author): God's answer to the angels is expanded by Adam's election, teaching him the names, and creating him with His hands: succession is bestowed by God, not earned through abundant worship.

positions.position: The detailed reply explains the earlier summary that God knows what the angels do not; a genuine summary and its detail have the same meaning.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): The detailed reply explains the earlier summary that God knows what the angels do not; a genuine summary and its detail have the same meaning.

positions.position: The wording need not add what the angels do know after what they do not know, since that is obvious; the emphasis is on the reach of God's knowledge beyond theirs.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR-FULL (author): The wording need not add what the angels do know after what they do not know, since that is obvious; the emphasis is on the reach of God's knowledge beyond theirs.

positions.position: Ibn Ishaq reads the phrase as God's knowledge of what was among them, which He had not disclosed to the angels: disobedience, corruption, and bloodshed.
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (ابن إسحاق): Ibn Ishaq reads the phrase as God's knowledge of what was among them, which He had not disclosed to the angels: disobedience, corruption, and bloodshed.

positions.position: Other proposed purposes are to expose angels' inability to encompass God's knowledge and to honor Adam in advance so they welcome him when created.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): Other proposed purposes are to expose angels' inability to encompass God's knowledge and to honor Adam in advance so they welcome him when created.

positions.position: God's knowledge of Adam also includes hidden faults unknown to angels: bodily dispositions shared with animals and vices produced by the commanding self when the spirit follows it without the discipline of sacred law.
positions.reasons: BURSEVI (author): God's knowledge of Adam also includes hidden faults unknown to angels: bodily dispositions shared with animals and vices produced by the commanding self when the spirit follows it without the discipline of sacred law.

positions.position: Successful vicegerency requires authority to manage the entrusted domain and the capacity and knowledge to do so; the preceding verse summarizes both through creation of the earth for people and God's knowledge.
positions.reasons: SAMARRAI-ASRAR (author): Successful vicegerency requires authority to manage the entrusted domain and the capacity and knowledge to do so; the preceding verse summarizes both through creation of the earth for people and God's knowledge.

positions.position: One explanation is that Adam's descendants will include obedient prophets, saints, and scholars.
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI-FULL (قيل): One explanation is that Adam's descendants will include obedient prophets, saints, and scholars.

positions.position: A further explanation is that humans will sin and God will forgive them.
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI-FULL (قيل): A further explanation is that humans will sin and God will forgive them.

positions.position: A further view takes the words to mean God's exclusive knowledge of how to manage people's interests.
positions.reasons: TABRISI (author): A further view takes the words to mean God's exclusive knowledge of how to manage people's interests.

positions.position: The shift from general address to the Prophet's particular address hints that he receives the greatest share of what follows; Abū Ḥayyān recalls his universal mission and precedence among prophets.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): The shift from general address to the Prophet's particular address hints that he receives the greatest share of what follows; Abū Ḥayyān recalls his universal mission and precedence among prophets.

positions.position: He argues that creation contains hidden realities: even the natural world, its narrowest and lowest domain, continually yields new unknowns as scientific inquiry uncovers facts.
positions.reasons: TABATABAI (author): He argues that creation contains hidden realities: even the natural world, its narrowest and lowest domain, continually yields new unknowns as scientific inquiry uncovers facts.

turns_on: Whether the hidden matter is Iblis, righteous descendants, Adam's fitness, forgiveness, or God's wider unseen knowledge.

question: What wisdom makes the successor's appointment fitting despite corruption?

positions.position: The interrogative is affirmative like the poet's 'Are you not the best riders?'
positions.reasons: AKHFASH (author): The interrogative is affirmative like the poet's 'Are you not the best riders?'

positions.position: Ibn Zayd interprets the angels’ question as amazement that God would create beings who disobey their creator, rather than as knowledge that this would certainly occur.
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (ابن زيد): Ibn Zayd interprets the angels’ question as amazement that God would create beings who disobey their creator, rather than as knowledge that this would certainly occur.

positions.position: The angels are the best of living beings and the most intelligent of creatures.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI-FULL (author): The angels are the best of living beings and the most intelligent of creatures.

positions.position: Al-Zajjaj gives the concise sense of the angels' words as declaring God free of evil.
positions.reasons: WAHIDI-BASIT (الزجاج): Al-Zajjaj gives the concise sense of the angels' words as declaring God free of evil.

positions.position: The angels declare God free of every evil and say, Glory and praise belong to God.
positions.reasons: WAHIDI-WAJIZ (author): The angels declare God free of every evil and say, Glory and praise belong to God.

positions.position: One proposed question is how God could create beings He knows will disbelieve, when all His acts are good and He cannot do wrong.
positions.reasons: JISHUMI (author): One proposed question is how God could create beings He knows will disbelieve, when all His acts are good and He cannot do wrong.

positions.position: Abū ʿAlī says God knows the interests involved and which location is best for angels and people.
positions.reasons: JISHUMI (أبو علي): Abū ʿAlī says God knows the interests involved and which location is best for angels and people.

positions.position: God’s answer implies He does not do evil; it is meaningful as an appeal to knowledge of governance and interests, leading Him to do what is best.
positions.reasons: JISHUMI (author): God’s answer implies He does not do evil; it is meaningful as an appeal to knowledge of governance and interests, leading Him to do what is best.

positions.position: God's answer points to the wisdom and benefit in His decision.
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI-FULL (author): God's answer points to the wisdom and benefit in His decision.

positions.position: This reading requires ellipsis: God knows future corruption and hidden interests, the angels implicitly compare their obedience with humans, and His reply supplies what they do not know.
positions.reasons: TABRISI (author): This reading requires ellipsis: God knows future corruption and hidden interests, the angels implicitly compare their obedience with humans, and His reply supplies what they do not know.

positions.position: God knows the interests better and does what is most fitting; the reply implies He does not perform evil, since otherwise it would have no force.
positions.reasons: TABRISI (author): God knows the interests better and does what is most fitting; the reply implies He does not perform evil, since otherwise it would have no force.

positions.position: They divide angels into celestial governors, related to spheres as human souls to bodies, and proximate angels absorbed in knowing, loving, and obeying God; some add good or evil angels governing the lower world.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (الفلاسفة): They divide angels into celestial governors, related to spheres as human souls to bodies, and proximate angels absorbed in knowing, loving, and obeying God; some add good or evil angels governing the lower world.

positions.position: Philosophers agree on celestial governors and angels devoted to God, while some also posit terrestrial angels governing the lower world, good as angels and evil as devils.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (الفلاسفة): Philosophers agree on celestial governors and angels devoted to God, while some also posit terrestrial angels governing the lower world, good as angels and evil as devils.

positions.position: Philosophers say evil necessarily accompanies worldly good, but good outweighs evil; abandoning much good to avoid little evil would be worse.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (الحكماء): Philosophers say evil necessarily accompanies worldly good, but good outweighs evil; abandoning much good to avoid little evil would be worse.

positions.position: On this account, good from the lower world's composition exceeds its evils, so wisdom requires creating it.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (الحكماء): On this account, good from the lower world's composition exceeds its evils, so wisdom requires creating it.

positions.position: Most Mu'tazilites and many jurists say angels can do both good and evil.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (جمهور المعتزلة وكثير من الفقهاء): Most Mu'tazilites and many jurists say angels can do both good and evil.

positions.position: The poet's phrase thawb al-muqaddas means a purified garment; prayer purifies a servant from sins and is entered in the worshipper's best state because it is the best deed.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL (author): The poet's phrase thawb al-muqaddas means a purified garment; prayer purifies a servant from sins and is entered in the worshipper's best state because it is the best deed.

positions.position: God’s announcement teaches consultation, honors the future inhabitant by naming him before creation, and displays his preponderant virtue through the angels’ question and answer; wisdom requires abundant good even when accompanied by lesser evil.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI-FULL (author): God’s announcement teaches consultation, honors the future inhabitant by naming him before creation, and displays his preponderant virtue through the angels’ question and answer; wisdom requires abundant good even when accompanied by lesser evil.

positions.position: God knows hidden wisdom: among humans will be prophets, saints, and scholars, along with matters the angels do not know.
positions.reasons: NASAFI-FULL (author): God knows hidden wisdom: among humans will be prophets, saints, and scholars, along with matters the angels do not know.

positions.position: Each angelic rank knows what is below and within itself but not above; they see the soul as evil-bearing intermediary between luminous spirit and dark body.
positions.reasons: QASHANI (author): Each angelic rank knows what is below and within itself but not above; they see the soul as evil-bearing intermediary between luminous spirit and dark body.

positions.position: He says the best explanation of the unspecified knowledge is God’s statement that he knows the unseen of the heavens and earth.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): He says the best explanation of the unspecified knowledge is God’s statement that he knows the unseen of the heavens and earth.

positions.position: The story of Adam is a manifest example that humanity is the intended purpose of this existence and that wisdom requires resurrection to a realm without disorder, where divine wisdom is fully evident.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (author): The story of Adam is a manifest example that humanity is the intended purpose of this existence and that wisdom requires resurrection to a realm without disorder, where divine wisdom is fully evident.

positions.position: God knows the wisdom of appointing Adam: his descendants include obedient and disobedient people, through whom merit and justice become manifest; creatures cannot know the Creator’s hidden governance.
positions.reasons: BURSEVI (author): God knows the wisdom of appointing Adam: his descendants include obedient and disobedient people, through whom merit and justice become manifest; creatures cannot know the Creator’s hidden governance.

positions.position: Wisdom permits a small evil when it prevents a much greater evil, as removing a diseased limb can save the whole body.
positions.reasons: BURSEVI (author): Wisdom permits a small evil when it prevents a much greater evil, as removing a diseased limb can save the whole body.

positions.position: Some gnostics identify the disputers as earth angels, jinn, and devils dominated by darkness, rather than heavenly angels who recognize the Perfect Human’s rank.
positions.reasons: BURSEVI (بعض العارفين): Some gnostics identify the disputers as earth angels, jinn, and devils dominated by darkness, rather than heavenly angels who recognize the Perfect Human’s rank.

positions.position: Those soul-born faults include vanity, ostentation, seeking reputation, envy, preferring worldly life, innovation, deviation, and holding evil opinions.
positions.reasons: BURSEVI (author): Those soul-born faults include vanity, ostentation, seeking reputation, envy, preferring worldly life, innovation, deviation, and holding evil opinions.

positions.position: The best-known interpretation identifies the khalīfa as Adam, matching the report, singular wording, and context; corruption and bloodshed are attributed to him causally or as potential in those succeeding him.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (المشهور): The best-known interpretation identifies the khalīfa as Adam, matching the report, singular wording, and context; corruption and bloodshed are attributed to him causally or as potential in those succeeding him.

positions.position: In a report transmitted from Ubadah ibn al-Samit from Abu Dharr, the Prophet calls “Glory be to God and praise be to Him” the best utterance God chose for His angels or servants; no grading is
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (أبو ذر عن النبي): In a report transmitted from Ubadah ibn al-Samit from Abu Dharr, the Prophet calls “Glory be to God and praise be to Him” the best utterance God chose for His angels or servants; no grading is stated.

positions.position: The angels understood the honor of vicegerency but feared the possible evil of giving a creature on earth such high discretionary authority.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): The angels understood the honor of vicegerency but feared the possible evil of giving a creature on earth such high discretionary authority.

positions.position: The following verse's teaching of Adam and demonstration of his distinction give detailed evidence for his fitness as steward, explaining what the angels did not know.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR-FULL (author): The following verse's teaching of Adam and demonstration of his distinction give detailed evidence for his fitness as steward, explaining what the angels did not know.

positions.position: Although 4:1 and 39:6 later describe Adam's creation and human reproduction, this passage concerns capacities, responsibilities, authority, and blessings bestowed on humanity.
positions.reasons: KURANYOLU-TEFSIR (author): Although 4:1 and 39:6 later describe Adam's creation and human reproduction, this passage concerns capacities, responsibilities, authority, and blessings bestowed on humanity.

positions.position: Alternatively, the angels may have witnessed Adam's creation and inferred from his material and spiritual traits that he could do both good and evil.
positions.reasons: KURANYOLU-TEFSIR (author): Alternatively, the angels may have witnessed Adam's creation and inferred from his material and spiritual traits that he could do both good and evil.

positions.position: God makes part of the wisdom clear in the following account by teaching Adam the names.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF-FULL (author): God makes part of the wisdom clear in the following account by teaching Adam the names.

positions.position: Alternatively, they affirmed God's divinity and wisdom to show they sought details rather than attacking Him.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Alternatively, they affirmed God's divinity and wisdom to show they sought details rather than attacking Him.

positions.position: God connects His acts to hidden causes and wisdom, yet no creature can claim entitlement through a cause: He creates causes and grants outcomes, and His will is the true original cause.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): God connects His acts to hidden causes and wisdom, yet no creature can claim entitlement through a cause: He creates causes and grants outcomes, and His will is the true original cause.

question: What does the exchange teach about praising oneself or seeking office?

positions.position: The angels privately claimed that no creation would surpass them in knowledge or honor; God tested that boast by teaching Adam the names and challenging them to name them.
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (الحسن وقتادة): The angels privately claimed that no creation would surpass them in knowledge or honor; God tested that boast by teaching Adam the names and challenging them to name them.

positions.position: Al-Rabi reports that the angels privately boasted of superior knowledge and honor; God taught Adam the names to show his superiority, exposing their public words and hidden claim.
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (الربيع بن أنس): Al-Rabi reports that the angels privately boasted of superior knowledge and honor; God taught Adam the names to show his superiority, exposing their public words and hidden claim.

positions.position: Pride in one's work and abundant worship makes ignorance one's home; the angels' boast led them to confess ignorance.
positions.reasons: SULAMI (بعضهم): Pride in one's work and abundant worship makes ignorance one's home; the angels' boast led them to confess ignorance.

positions.position: One view says the angels were not objecting or boasting of their deeds; they were expressing wonder and seeking the wisdom behind the decision.
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI-FULL (قيل): One view says the angels were not objecting or boasting of their deeds; they were expressing wonder and seeking the wisdom behind the decision.

question: How is the first person yāʾ in innī aʿlam read?

positions.position: The first person yāʾ is opened
positions.reasons: IBNMUJAHID (أبو عمرو): Abū ʿAmr opens the first-person yāʾ after a kasra before an open or kasra hamza attached to a noun or verb, unless the letter is lengthened. IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA (author): Opening the possessive yāʾ treats it as a built pronoun like hāʾ or kāf; the vowel is fitting after the preceding kasra. IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA (القراء): One group opens yāʾ before a hamza with fatḥa but uses sukūn before ḍamma or kasra, avoiding those heavier vowel combinations. IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA (القراء): Another group uses sukūn before ḍamma, the heaviest vowel, but opens yāʾ before the other hamzas. FARISI-HUJJA (أبو عمرو): Abū ʿAmr opens the attached yāʾ after a kasra before an open or kasra hamza; this rule includes إني أعلم. FARISI-HUJJA (أبو عمرو): He does not open the yāʾ before a hamza with ḍamma, as in the cited examples; his opening rule is restricted to the open and kasra hamza. FARISI-HUJJA (author): The case for opening the attached yāʾ is that its original vowel is fatḥa, parallel to the addressee kāf, which is also opened. FARISI-HUJJA (أبو عمرو): Abū ʿAmr’s reason for opening yāʾ before a light hamza is that hamza can induce fatḥa in otherwise unopen forms such as يقرأ and يبرأ. WAHIDI-BASIT (أبو عمرو): Abu Amr and Ibn Kathir pronounce the first-person yāʾ with fatḥa before an open hamza, as in innī aʿlam and innī arā; Abu Amr also does so before a kasra hamza, and Nafi adds cases before a ḍamma hamza. BAGHAWI-FULL (أهل الحجاز والبصرة): The Hijaz and Basra readers open the ya in inni a'lam and in most possessive ya forms before an alif with fatḥa; readers differ on the detailed exceptions. NASHR (المدنيان وابن كثير وأبو عمرو): The two Medinan readers, Ibn Kathīr, and Abū ʿAmr open the yāʾ in إني أعلم at both occurrences. QIRAAT-ER (author): The canonical innīya with fatḥa and innī with sukūn differ phonologically in pause or connection, with no semantic change.

positions.position: The first person yāʾ is omitted
positions.reasons: IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA (القراء): A third group deletes the possessive yāʾ entirely and relies on the remaining vowel.

positions.position: Ibn Kathīr does not follow one consistent rule for these attached yāʾ vowels; his individual cases are listed separately by sūra.

positions.position: Surplus letters may be dropped without changing intended construction.

positions.position: Angels sought knowledge rather than objected, or disliked disobedience after the jinn's example.

positions.position: On this reconstruction, angels generalized from some descendants’ corruption to all of them; God had concealed that many would obey, reform the earth, preserve blood and attain honor.
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (author): On this reconstruction, angels generalized from some descendants’ corruption to all of them; God had concealed that many would obey, reform the earth, preserve blood and attain honor.

positions.position: Sukūn avoids the heaviness of a vowel on yāʾ and restores the pronoun's underlying built form.
positions.reasons: IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA (author): Sukūn avoids the heaviness of a vowel on yāʾ and restores the pronoun's underlying built form.

positions.position: Although vowels on weak letters are often avoided, fatḥa is acceptable: yāʾ in al-qāḍī is inflected with fatḥa, and accusative غَوَاشٍ retains its yāʾ.

positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA (author): The moving feminine/plural nūn in فعلن and يفعلن is another pronominal parallel; despite an objection that it moves only to avoid adjacent sukūns, its likeness to kāf and tāʾ supports movement.

positions.position: A khalīfa is one who takes another’s place, from the verb khalafa, “to succeed someone.”
positions.reasons: MAWARDI-FULL (author): A khalīfa is one who takes another’s place, from the verb khalafa, “to succeed someone.”

positions.position: The angels may have asked to learn the wisdom, not objected: after the jinn were removed, they occupied earth and asked why corrupting humans would replace them.
positions.reasons: WAHIDI-BASIT (الزجاج): The angels may have asked to learn the wisdom, not objected: after the jinn were removed, they occupied earth and asked why corrupting humans would replace them.

positions.position: An unnamed poet’s line supports ellipsis: after a conditional أينما, the understood verb ذهب is omitted.
positions.reasons: JISHUMI (الشاعر): An unnamed poet’s line supports ellipsis: after a conditional أينما, the understood verb ذهب is omitted.

positions.position: Al-Mahdawi parses the accusative as an answer to the question; Ibn Atiyya prefers the wa al-sarf analysis.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL (المهدوي): Al-Mahdawi parses the accusative as an answer to the question; Ibn Atiyya prefers the wa al-sarf analysis.

positions.position: A fourth objection infers angels are punished because 74:31 calls them keepers of Hell and 2:39 describes its eternal inhabitants.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (المخالفون): A fourth objection infers angels are punished because 74:31 calls them keepers of Hell and 2:39 describes its eternal inhabitants.

positions.position: The relative pronoun man is the first object of jaʿala and fiha stands in for the second; yufsidu agrees with man in form, though a non-Qur'anic plural yufsidoon may agree by meaning.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL (author): The relative pronoun man is the first object of jaʿala and fiha stands in for the second; yufsidu agrees with man in form, though a non-Qur'anic plural yufsidoon may agree by meaning.

positions.position: Al-Jawhari explains that hajjaj bayt Allah is genitive by annexation for women who made pilgrimage, but accusative if no pilgrimage occurred and tanwin is intended.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL (الجوهري): Al-Jawhari explains that hajjaj bayt Allah is genitive by annexation for women who made pilgrimage, but accusative if no pilgrimage occurred and tanwin is intended.

positions.position: The angels express surprise that a corruptor be appointed to cultivate and repair the earth, or that sinful people replace its obedient inhabitants; they seek the hidden wisdom like learners seeking clarification, not objecting to God.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI-FULL (author): The angels express surprise that a corruptor be appointed to cultivate and repair the earth, or that sinful people replace its obedient inhabitants; they seek the hidden wisdom like learners seeking clarification, not objecting to God.

positions.position: The construction is like 5:61, where entering with disbelief means entering while disbelieving.
positions.reasons: NASAFI-FULL (author): The construction is like 5:61, where entering with disbelief means entering while disbelieving.

positions.position: The predicate after qāla is introduced by anna to stress that the reported statement is certain to occur.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): The predicate after qāla is introduced by anna to stress that the reported statement is certain to occur.

positions.position: Sībawayh says that when the active participle operates, using it as an operative form is better than annexing it to its object.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (سيبويه): Sībawayh says that when the active participle operates, using it as an operative form is better than annexing it to its object.

positions.position: Al-Kisāʾī regards the operative and annexed constructions as equal; Abū Ḥayyān chooses annexation as better.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (الكسائي): Al-Kisāʾī regards the operative and annexed constructions as equal; Abū Ḥayyān chooses annexation as better.

positions.position: One view makes jaʿala mean create, taking one object; Abū Rawq holds this, close to reports from al-Ḥasan and Qatāda.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (أبو روق): One view makes jaʿala mean create, taking one object; Abū Rawq holds this, close to reports from al-Ḥasan and Qatāda.

positions.position: A second view, held by al-Farrāʾ, makes jaʿala mean turn into, taking two objects, with fī al-arḍ supplying the second; al-Zamakhsharī gives only this view.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (الفراء): A second view, held by al-Farrāʾ, makes jaʿala mean turn into, taking two objects, with fī al-arḍ supplying the second; al-Zamakhsharī gives only this view.

positions.position: Views differ on Adam's delegated task: judging with truth and justice, or cultivating the earth through farming, construction, and canals.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): Views differ on Adam's delegated task: judging with truth and justice, or cultivating the earth through farming, construction, and canals.

positions.position: The Basrans allow omission of the subject in a verbal noun construction; unlike some grammarians, Abū Ḥayyān says this is not forbidden because generic nouns do not take pronouns.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): The Basrans allow omission of the subject in a verbal noun construction; unlike some grammarians, Abū Ḥayyān says this is not forbidden because generic nouns do not take pronouns.

positions.position: Islamic doctrine holds angels immune from sin and objection; this premise led exegetes to interpret their words in a linguistically plausible way, against a minority of Hashwiyya.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): Islamic doctrine holds angels immune from sin and objection; this premise led exegetes to interpret their words in a linguistically plausible way, against a minority of Hashwiyya.

positions.position: He insists that the apparent reading is the present-tense verb أعلم and warns against imposing unattested grammatical patterns on Quranic wording.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): He insists that the apparent reading is the present-tense verb أعلم and warns against imposing unattested grammatical patterns on Quranic wording.

positions.position: من may be a relative pronoun, leaving the following clause without an independent syntactic position; as an indefinite it makes the clause accusative.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (author): من may be a relative pronoun, leaving the following clause without an independent syntactic position; as an indefinite it makes the clause accusative.

positions.position: Grammarians disagree whether a verbal noun used in place of a verb can contain an implicit pronoun.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (author): Grammarians disagree whether a verbal noun used in place of a verb can contain an implicit pronoun.

positions.position: إني contracts إنني by dropping one of three adjacent nūns; the correct view deletes the middle nūn rather than the nūn of protection.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (author): إني contracts إنني by dropping one of three adjacent nūns; the correct view deletes the middle nūn rather than the nūn of protection.

positions.position: The angels’ question sought guidance about what they did not know, not denial or objection; Ibn Jarir prefers this explanation.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR-FULL (ابن جرير): The angels’ question sought guidance about what they did not know, not denial or objection; Ibn Jarir prefers this explanation.

positions.position: The catalogue gives 139 instances for mīm, 70 for nūn, and 18 for wāw, split into 13 after a ḍamma and five after sukūn.
positions.reasons: NASHR (author): The catalogue gives 139 instances for mīm, 70 for nūn, and 18 for wāw, split into 13 after a ḍamma and five after sukūn.

positions.position: Qawl is the outward arrangement of verbal forms, like the joining of visible forms; the heart apprehends speech through the ear as it apprehends visible things through sight.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (author): Qawl is the outward arrangement of verbal forms, like the joining of visible forms; the heart apprehends speech through the ear as it apprehends visible things through sight.

positions.position: The angels first submitted, then objected that a successor would corrupt earth; after God turned from them, they circled the Throne six years seeking forgiveness and repenting.
positions.reasons: DURR-FULL (أنس): The angels first submitted, then objected that a successor would corrupt earth; after God turned from them, they circled the Throne six years seeking forgiveness and repenting.

positions.position: The recipient phrase routinely comes first in this construction because the quoted speech is often long, while its placement adds emphasis and anticipation.
positions.reasons: BURSEVI (author): The recipient phrase routinely comes first in this construction because the quoted speech is often long, while its placement adds emphasis and anticipation.

positions.position: Bursevī illustrates mediation with cartilage between bone and flesh, a minister between ruler and subjects, and dry wood between fire and wet wood.
positions.reasons: BURSEVI (author): Bursevī illustrates mediation with cartilage between bone and flesh, a minister between ruler and subjects, and dry wood between fire and wet wood.

positions.position: The angels’ objection and dispute before the wise Creator is excused because of His perfect wisdom and workmanship.
positions.reasons: BURSEVI (author): The angels’ objection and dispute before the wise Creator is excused because of His perfect wisdom and workmanship.

positions.position: The plural's feminine agreement reflects the semantic feminine of a group, as grammarians say every collective is feminine by construing it as a community.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): The plural's feminine agreement reflects the semantic feminine of a group, as grammarians say every collective is feminine by construing it as a community.

positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): أعلم is an imperfect verb here; construing it as the elative adjective “more knowing” is not an acceptable reading of the Qur'an.

positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): The lām in “for You” may mark purpose with nuqaddisu, be a transitive marker as in “I prostrated to God,” indicate clarification, or be extra with the object understood as the prepositional phrase.

positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): If “Your praise” is construed as an active genitive, it figuratively means God's enabling and guidance, denying any implication of angelic self-congratulation.

positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (author): Al-Ṭabarī explicitly says this is his description of how the report may be interpreted, not the interpretation he chooses for the verse itself.

positions.position: Qatada reports that God sought the angels’ counsel about Adam; they knew bloodshed and earthly corruption were especially hateful to God, while Adam’s line would also include prophets, messengers, righteous people and people of Paradise.

positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (author): Al-Tabari says knowledge of past events is reliable only through transmission that rules out collusion, lying, error and forgetfulness; the cited reports do not meet that standard, so the text-supported interpretation is preferable.

positions.reasons: ZAJJAJ (author): The report about Adam and the angels’ prostration proves Muhammad’s prophethood to scriptural communities: Arabs did not know it, while scripture readers or revelation did.

positions.position: In the reported account, God gave the angels leave to ask about the matter.
positions.reasons: ZAJJAJ (author): In the reported account, God gave the angels leave to ask about the matter.

positions.position: Ibn Sabit reports that the earth spread from Mecca and angels first circumambulated the House; he glosses the location of the khalifa as Mecca.

positions.position: Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Ali reports that the angel al-Sijill saw Adam's creation and affairs in the Preserved Tablet and told Harut and Marut; they then spoke from a sense of superiority over the angels.
positions.reasons: IBNABIHATIM (محمد بن علي): Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Ali reports that the angel al-Sijill saw Adam's creation and affairs in the Preserved Tablet and told Harut and Marut; they then spoke from a sense of superiority over the angels.

positions.position: The continuation of the quoted poem concludes the example for omitting the connective fa; its gloss is “so I was their neighbor.”
positions.reasons: THALABI (author): The continuation of the quoted poem concludes the example for omitting the connective fa; its gloss is “so I was their neighbor.”

positions.reasons: THALABI (author): One reported explanation is that among those appointed on earth will be prophets, saints, scholars, and righteous people.

positions.position: Sibawayh reports a pronunciation with fatḥa in سبوح قدوس; ḍamma is more common, while fatḥa is more analogical.
positions.reasons: TABRISI (سيبويه): Sibawayh reports a pronunciation with fatḥa in سبوح قدوس; ḍamma is more common, while fatḥa is more analogical.

positions.position: Such concise ellipsis is Qur'anic eloquence when the remaining wording signals what was omitted; the segment introduces al-Shanfara's poem as evidence.
positions.reasons: TABRISI (author): Such concise ellipsis is Qur'anic eloquence when the remaining wording signals what was omitted; the segment introduces al-Shanfara's poem as evidence.

positions.position: A report places Noah, Hud, Salih, and Shuʿayb's graves between Zamzam and the Corner and Station.
positions.reasons: TABRISI (author): A report places Noah, Hud, Salih, and Shuʿayb's graves between Zamzam and the Corner and Station.

positions.reasons: TABRISI (author): Al-Shanfara's poem omits “do not bury me, but leave me to be eaten by the hyena”; the intended continuation is recoverable.

positions.position: Abu Dawud's poem omits “if you disapprove, leave”; the omitted clause follows from the conditional context.
